newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian leaders seek compromise to avoid chaos.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian leaders seek compromise to avoid chaos.

text.p: Bulgaria's leaders struggled on Friday to find a compromise to pull the country back from the brink of political and economic chaos after 26 days of mass protests against the beleaguered Socialist government.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the ruling Socialists' nominee to form a new government, offered to stand aside and let liberal President Petar Stoyanov appoint a coalition team.
Dobrev, given a mandate to form a government earlier this week, said he would be willing to give up his efforts for the sake of consensus between warring political factions.
"I think the country now needs a constitutional government on a very wide political base," he told Reuters in an interview.
"I don't mind if it is formed under the leadership of the president," he said. "I am ready to return my mandate if such a government is formed."

Stoyanov, a divorce lawyer who took office last week, has called on all parties to reject the mandate and join a coalition cabinet to adopt urgently needed economic reforms. Elections would then be held.
Under the constitution he was obliged to give the mandate first to the Socialists, as the largest party in the 240-seat parliament.
Returning on Friday from talks with European Union and NATO leaders in Brussels, Stoyanov renewed his call for Dobrev to return the mandate to help revolve the crisis.
"The decent exit is really for Mr Dobrev to give up this mandate," Stoyanov told reporters.
The two men will meet later on Friday but the key to the crisis is now held by the opposition parties, which have said they would never except joining in a coalition led by Dobrev.

Bulgaria's economic and political crisis intensified after Stoyanov handed the Socialists a crushing presidential election defeat last November, reflecting widespread public rejection of Socialist policies.

The scale of that defeat forced prime minister Zhan Zidenov to resign in December and left the country in political limbo while inflation has soared to 50 percent a month and the lev has gone into a freefall.

The Socialists were elected to a four-year term in December 1994. But students, opposition parties and workers have joined forces during nearly a month of protests to demand an immediate general election.
Protesters kept up anti-government strikes and blockades on Friday. Demonstrators at Doupnitsa, south of Sofia, blockaded the main road to the Greek border for a third day.
Students, who have maintained festive themes during daily protests, shifted to disrupting traffic on the main Eagles' Bridge on the outskirts of the capital for a second day.
Opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) in the second city of Plovdiv said protesters planned to use buses to block the highway from Sofia to Turkey.

One-hour stoppages were reported at schools and factories around the country. Police set up barricades near the UDF headquarters in Sofia in anticipation of possible protests by young Socialists on Friday.
The Sofia circus was putting on a special performance for students, whose colourful, inventive daily protests rely on humour rather than confrontation.
The students then plan their daily march, and to join the main opposition rally at the Alexander Nevsky cathedral.
Parliament debated a stopgap budget bill drawn up by the outgoing cabinet to permit a doubling of state salaries to take account of soaring inflation.
The lev, in a freefall, was quoted at 1,730-1,900 on the interbank market on Friday compared to 1,530-1,590 at the close on Thursday.
